Chapter 1 Randomization and Random Samples Is a sample statistic statistically higher or lower than a population mean? We need a random sample in this scenario. Acock (2023) uses the example of a small liberal art college about selectivity compared to the population. The mean score for a small liberal arts college for math and reading was \(\bar{x}=1180\) while the population average SAT score is \(\mu=1080\). Can the liberal arts school say that there selectivity is higher than the average college? We can test the example above with a one-group test for means or proportions. Does a treatment has an impact on the treatment group? We need randomization into treatment and control in this scenario. Acock (2023) uses the example of a reading program for preschool children. There is a randomization of preschool students in and out of the reading program. On a outcome of 0-100 point scale, the children in the control group had an average score of \(\bar{y}=71.3\) with a standard deviation of \(sd=10.4\). In the treatment group, the average score was \(\bar{y}=82.5\) and \(sd=9.9\). It seems like the reading program had an impact, but we would need to test for statistical significant. We can use a two-group test for means or proportions for this example. 1.1 Random Samples Stata makes random samples and randomization straightforward and easy. We can implement random sampling without replacement with the sample command. There are many ways to implement random assignment, but we’ll cover a simple way to do so. Let’s say we have pre-SAT scores before treatment with \(\mu=1000\) and \(\sigma=50\). We randomly assign into two groups for a program to prepare for the SAT. However, we will discuss two-group tests to test the null hypothesis that these two groups are similar. 1.3 Significance level of \(p=0.05\) I want to focus on Acock’s (2023) discussion of the significance level of \(p=0.05\). We test our null hypothesis, \(H_0\) with a one-tailed or two-tailed test. How do we know when to reject \(H_0\)? The rule of thumb for statistical analysis has been when \(p < 0.05\). We say that we reject the null hypothesis at the \(5\%\) level. Some researchers use \(p < 0.01\) to say that we reject the null hypothesis at the \(1\%\) level or \(p < 0.001\) to say that we reject the null hypothesis at the \(0.1\%\) level. We may find \(p < 0.05\) just due to the fact that our \(N\) is extremely large. We may find statistical significance, but is it practical? We may find \(p < 0.05\) but our assumptions have been violated. (This is a preview for Econ 645 and Econ 672). Therefore, we risk rejecting a true null beyond our 5% level due to the bias. We may find \(p < 0.05\) if try to data mine and cherry pick results. Economist try to prevent cherry picking with extensive sensitivity and robustness tests. (Have you seen the length of online appendices?) Here are some of my thoughts on \(p < 0.05\) Always have a healthy skepticism that your assumptions have been satisfied. Think about the arbitrariness of \(p=0.051\) and \(p=0.049\). Don’t cherry pick results. Run sensitivity tests to try to break your results.

Chapter 3 Exercises 3.1 Randomization We will create a random sample from a random number generator. Step Create a blank file with 1000 observations Generate an id variable based on the row number. Set a seed to 91925 Create a variable called wages with a random number generator with \(\mu=1500\) and \(\sigma=500\) Summarize wages. What is the mean, minimum, and maximum? Generate a new random number called random_num. Sort ascending using random_um and create a new ranking variable. Create a new variable called treatment. Those 500 and below are set at 0 and those at 501 to 1000 are set at 1 Label the treatment variable 0 “Control” 1 “Treatment”. Use a \(t\)-test to test the null hypothesis \(\mu_{(control)}-\mu_{(treatment)}=0\) What do you conclude? 3.2 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth Do Latino families have more have more children than other ethnic groups? Load the file called “nlsy97_chapter7.dta” to answer the question. Step: First summarize hh18_97 which is the number of children under 18 Next, tabulate ethnic97 which is a binary for Latino/Hispanic Test the null hypothesis \(H_{0}: \mu_{(Latino)}-\mu_{(Non-Latino)}=0\) What do you conclude? 3.3 General Social Survey Are women more likely to say that abortion is okay under any circumstances than men? Load the file called “gss2002_chapter7.dta”. Steps First, tabulate abany Next, tabulate sex Then do a cross-tabulation on abany and sex Use the prtest command on abany and sex. What happened? We need to recode our variable into a binary. Generate a new variable based off of abany and label No 0 and Yes 1. Finally, test the null hypothesis: \(p_{(women)}-p_{(men)}-1\) What do you conclude?
